title: AI is hard to detect game exploits
author: iron_grim_games
selftext:
It's probably a small issue but maybe some of you could use that for your projects.

  
While i'm developing Frontline: Hold the Line, i realised that AI is good to detect bugs or optimize the game. But for for game exploits, its really bad. For example, my game is about building a defense to enemy waves with different types units. While designing the tutorial, i was discussing it with Claude, and the suggestion of it like decreasing enemy power for first 3 waves at tutorial. But thats obviously creates an exploit opportunity for players; an ambitous player easly starts with every run with tutorial for getting free command points (game money), then continue to real run after that. Claude could not realised that until i mentioned it.

  
So, if you are using AI to asisst your coding or modelling, its ok, but for game design, we still need heavy mind work of humans.

comments.author: EC36339
comments.body:
AI may have limited capabilities in game design (it's not a god or anything), but you haven't even tried to really leverage it properly.

For example, just from the top of my head, I would try...
* Adversarial review: Have agents deliberately try to find exploits. Let them interact with agents who try to prevent exploits in a loop.
* Simulation: Let agents play the game, or a pseudo game which implements the rules that are relevant, but turn-based, or something similar.

This won't magically build the perfect game with no human involvement, but it's way better than a discussion with an agent, and with human supervision and creativity in the loop, it's probably better than just human game designers without AI assistance. It's definitely faster.

Many "AI can't do this" problems can't be done by AI simply because there's no feedback loop. For example AI gets a lot better at graphics programming if you just give it the ability to take screenshots and run benchmarks.
